extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy, ethics, and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's evaluative principles about happiness, virtue, legislation, and education as presented in a philosophical treatise. Focuses on criteria for the best life, the formation of virtue, and the nature and requirements of statesmanship and laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as contemplative speculation (theoria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness must be a kind of Contemplative Speculation; the life of pure intellect (contemplation) is the highest form of Happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: contemplative activity is self-sufficient, chosen for its own sake, pleasant in itself, and akin to the life of the gods; human happiness is co-extensive with the act of contemplation and is most complete when life attains sufficient duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficiency as a criterion of the chief good
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief good (Happiness) should be Self-Sufficient — the thing which, when isolated, makes life desirable and lacking in nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemplative life is presented as most Self-Sufficient because it requires fewer external relations than practical virtues which need social contexts, resources, or opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice-worthiness for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest activity should be chosen for its own sake and not as a means to further ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemplation is valued because it aims at no end beyond itself, unlike practical actions (war, statecraft) which aim at further ends such as power or civic goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for rest and continuity/unweariedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect Happiness involves qualities like capacity of rest, continuity of activity, and unweariedness compatible with human infirmity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemplative activity admits of rest and sustained exercise in a way practical and warlike activities do not; this endurance contributes to it being the highest happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic pleasure augmenting activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest activity contains its own pleasure which aids and increases the activity itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike practical virtues whose actions aim at outcomes, contemplation yields pleasure that is part of the activity, reinforcing that activity's excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: External goods are necessary but only to a moderate degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Human speculation requires some external goods (health, nourishment, bodily conditions), but not large or excessive possessions to achieve high Happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Solon’s picture of the happy as moderately supplied; the point is that sufficient means to perform virtuous action suffice — extreme wealth or power is unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical virtues require social conditions and external aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtues (justice, courage, liberality, self-mastery) require society, other people, or external circumstances for their working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: brave actions need power/opportunity, liberal actions need money, self-mastery requires temptation to display restraint — therefore practical virtue depends more on external goods than contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Wisdom (phronesis) unified with moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical Wisdom and Excellence of Moral Character are closely united: moral virtues are right when they accord with Practical Wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical Wisdom supplies principles in accordance with moral virtues, guiding right action in concrete situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue consists of both moral choice and actions; perfection requires both
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue involves both the internal moral choice and the outward actions; both are necessary for the perfection of virtuous character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions require many external things; hence perfection of virtuous action requires the right internal disposition together with enabling circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of virtue requires nature, custom (habituation), and teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: The formation of a virtuous character is ascribed variously to Nature, Custom (habituation), and Teaching; habituation and upbringing are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words and precept alone are often insufficient; the mind must be predisposed (affinity to virtue) and trained by laws and practice from youth, including regulated food and manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law and public institutions should regulate upbringing and habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Because most people respond more to compulsion than to reason, lawgivers ought to regulate food, manner of living, and habits to form virtue in citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal regulation (as in the Lacedæmonian example) should aim to make virtuous habits customary; family/private training complements but law has broader compulsory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of honor and punishment in legal education
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawgivers should employ the sense of honour to exhort those with promising dispositions and employ chastisement/punishments for the baser sort, expelling the incurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishments should be contrary to the pleasures the punished value; honour motivates the well-trained, while pain restrains those amenable only to compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law has authoritative, impersonal force superior to paternal rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Law, as emanating from Practical Wisdom and Intellect, possesses compulsory power and is not the object of personal enmity the way human authority may be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Law's impersonal authority makes it effective in enforcing right rules where paternal or individual rule lacks strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private training better for individual cases; public for general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Private care/training can attend more exactly to individual circumstances, while public systems provide general maxims and standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: a physician treating a particular case vs. general medical rules; in arts like boxing or healing particulars require individualized attention though general principles are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statesmanship requires both knowledge (theory) and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Political science and legislation are not purely rhetorical or merely practical; acquiring the art of statesmanship requires both theoretical understanding and practical experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Sophists: those who teach statesmanship but do not practice it lack real knowledge; analogy to physicians and painters — those who perform and teach should coincide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collections of laws aid only those qualified to judge; lists do not make legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: Compilations of constitutions and laws are useful to those who can speculate and judge, but mere selection of famous laws does not itself constitute the skill of legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like medical compilations, treatises assist trained practitioners; the unqualified cannot derive legislative art merely from reading laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate existing polities empirically to determine good constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine what constitution and regulations are best, one should collect precedents and examine what preserves or destroys communities and particular constitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: gather fragments of predecessors' statements and study polities to ascertain causes of success or failure, then synthesize best regulations adapted to each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical moral concerns are judged by facts and actual life
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth in matters of moral action is grounded in facts and lived experience rather than mere speculative theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theories must harmonize with actual life; when at variance they are mere speculation — hence empirical reference to human conduct is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemplative life is nearer to divine and therefore pre-eminent
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the divine is characterized by contemplation, the life according to pure intellect in humans is comparatively divine and thus the most excellent life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: we should strive, 'so far as we can, make ourselves like immortals' and orient our actions to the highest Principle in us; the gods’ working is essentially contemplative, not practical.
